home.headline: Half a can of cola leaves your stomach in about half an hour. Half a burger with fries takes over four hours.
home.lead: LifePeek shows why. Pick a meal, press Play and watch it travel through the body: how fast it leaves the stomach, where the sugar, protein, fat and fibre go, and how blood sugar and energy respond. Keep one meal to compare it with the next.
home.previewCaption: Food still in the stomach after eating — computed by the LifePeek model

how.title: How it works
how.computed: Nothing is typed in by hand
how.computedBody: Each food is described by its nutrients and glycemic index, taken from published tables. The model works out how fast it leaves the stomach and how blood sugar responds.
how.honestBody: People differ. Times in the intestines and blood sugar are shown as typical ranges for healthy adults, with the source for every input.
how.classBody: Projector mode, English and Hindi, keys for a presentation clicker, works offline once loaded, and a link that reopens the exact same meals.

mouth.name: Mouth
mouth.what: Teeth cut and grind food while the tongue mixes it with saliva into a soft ball called a bolus.
mouth.chemistry: Salivary amylase starts breaking starch into smaller sugars. Lingual lipase begins on fat, but very little happens yet.
mouth.fact: Your salivary glands make roughly 1 to 1.5 litres of saliva a day.

esophagus.name: Food pipe (oesophagus)
esophagus.what: Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push each swallow down to the stomach in a few seconds.
esophagus.chemistry: No digestion happens here. Mucus helps the bolus slide.
esophagus.fact: Peristalsis works even upside down — astronauts can swallow in space.

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.what: The stomach stores the meal, churns it with acid into a thick liquid called chyme, and lets it out a little at a time through the pyloric sphincter.
stomach.chemistry: Hydrochloric acid unfolds proteins and kills many microbes. Pepsin starts cutting proteins into shorter chains. Liquids leave first; solids must be ground to tiny pieces before they can leave.
stomach.absorbed: Very little — some water, alcohol and a few drugs.
stomach.fact: The more calories a meal has, the more slowly it leaves: the small intestine signals the stomach to deliver only a few calories per minute.

smallIntestine.name: Small intestine
smallIntestine.what: Chyme moves through about 3 metres of narrow tube. Its lining is folded into millions of villi that give it a huge surface for absorption.
smallIntestine.chemistry: Bile from the liver breaks fat into tiny droplets. Pancreatic enzymes — amylase, lipase, trypsin — and enzymes on the villi finish breaking food into sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.
smallIntestine.absorbed: Most nutrients and most of the water are absorbed here into the blood and lymph.
smallIntestine.fact: The villi and microvilli give the small intestine a surface area of around 30 square metres — about half a badminton court.

largeIntestine.name: Large intestine
largeIntestine.what: What could not be digested — mainly fibre — moves slowly through the colon and is stored until it leaves the body.
largeIntestine.chemistry: Gut bacteria ferment fibre, making gases and short-chain fatty acids that feed the colon’s own cells. Some vitamins, such as vitamin K, are made by bacteria here.
largeIntestine.absorbed: Most of the remaining water and salts.
largeIntestine.fact: This is the slowest part of the journey: commonly a day or more.

teach.title: Using LifePeek in class
teach.lead: LifePeek is built for a projector and a 40-minute lesson on nutrition and digestion (for example, the “Life Processes” chapter).
steps: Predict: ask the class which leaves the stomach first, a can of cola or a burger with fries, and which raises blood sugar more.
Open cola with burger + fries kept (the first ready lesson below) and press Play. The dashed grey line is the kept burger.
Press Page Down (or the presentation clicker) to jump from one key moment to the next. At each one, read the line under the body: where the food is now.
Read blood sugar at 1 hour from the Blood sugar graph: drag the timeline to 1 h, and press B to bring that graph to the front.
Finish with energy at 3 hours: is more energy coming in from the meal, or being used by the body? Press E for the Energy graph.
tips: Projector mode (top right) shows one big graph at a time: press S, B or E to switch between Stomach, Blood sugar and Energy.
Open the app once on Wi-Fi; after that it works offline.
Every screen has its own link: save it in your notes to reopen the exact setup.
Every graph has “Show as table” for students using screen readers, and every control works from the keyboard (press ? for the list of keys).
teach.lessonsLead: Each opens in projector mode on a laptop, paused at its first key moment, on the graph it is about. Press Play, or Page Down for the next key moment.

teach.qrCaption: Students scan this code with the phone camera to open LifePeek. No login, nothing to install.
answers: About 35 minutes (30 to 40 is right): the ring on the stomach graph, or its marker on the timeline.
Cola, about 8 times faster: a drink starts leaving straight away, and it has fewer calories than a burger with fries.
About 111 mg/dL (105 to 115). Its highest, about 121, was at 35 minutes.
The body is using more: almost nothing is coming in from the cola, while the body uses about 63 kcal an hour.

science.title: Science and sources
science.lead: What the model computes, what it assumes, and where every number comes from.
science.modelBody: Stomach emptying is computed from the meal. Drinks start leaving straight away — water within minutes, drinks with calories at about 2 kcal per minute. Solid food is first ground for about 20 minutes, then leaves at about 1.4 kcal per minute, so meals with more calories take longer. (In the model a bigger meal empties at the same rate; real stomachs speed up a little for big meals.) Blood sugar is computed from the carbohydrate being absorbed, its glycemic index, and the slowing effect of fat and protein.
science.fixedBody: Time in the small and large intestine varies far more between people than between meals, so LifePeek uses typical published values and shows the range.
limits: Models a healthy adult only — not children, pregnancy, diabetes or digestive illness.
Blood sugar is a typical shape, not a prediction for any one person.
Exercise, sleep, stress and drinks with the meal all change real results.
Glycemic index values for mixed and home-cooked dishes vary between studies.
Fibre isn't modelled on its own: its slowing effect on blood sugar shows up through each food's glycemic index.

about.title: About LifePeek
about.lead: Compare what happens to two meals inside your body. Free, no login, works offline once loaded.
about.maker: LifePeek is made by {{name}}. Every number in it is cited, and every report of a mistake is checked against published sources.
about.medical: LifePeek is an educational model of a typical healthy adult. It does not model children, pregnancy, diabetes or digestive illness. Its numbers are typical ranges, not measurements of any person, and must not be used to choose a diet, treat an illness or change medicine. If you have diabetes or any health concern, talk to a doctor or a qualified dietitian.
about.sources: Each food is described only by cited values: its nutrients from USDA FoodData Central or the Indian Nutrient Databank, and, where it applies, its glycemic index from the International GI tables (Atkinson et al. 2008). The model computes everything else.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.summary: **Short version: LifePeek does not ask for, collect or store anything about you.** There are no accounts, no logins, no ads, no cookies and no tracking.

sections.title: What stays on your device
intro: LifePeek saves a few things **in your own browser only**. They are never sent to us:
items: your language (English or Hindi), whether Projector mode is on, and whether you have closed the "not medical advice" note;
whether you have chosen less movement on screen (reduced motion);
whether you have switched off the letter-key shortcuts;
a one-time note that the page has just reloaded after an update error (deleted when you close the tab);
a copy of the app, so it works offline in class;
the meals you pick are kept in the page address (the link). A share link contains only the meals, nothing about you.
outro: You can delete all of this by clearing the site data for lifepeek.vercel.app in your browser settings.

sections.title: Reporting a mistake
intro: When you press **Report a mistake**, LifePeek opens a **GitHub issue** in a new tab with your report already filled in. **Nothing is sent to us. Your report text reaches GitHub only inside the link that opens the form, and nothing is published until you press Submit there.** You choose whether to send it.
items: GitHub issues are **public**. Anyone can read them.
You need a GitHub account, and GitHub only allows accounts for people aged 13 and over. If you are younger, ask your teacher to send the report.
GitHub's own privacy statement applies to your account and the issue: https://docs.github.com/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement
**Don't type your name, school, phone number, email or any health information** in the report. Just say what is wrong and, if you can, where the right number comes from.
If you posted something by mistake, ask us (see "Contact" below) and we will delete the issue.

sections.title: Hosting
intro: The app is served by Vercel, a web hosting company. Like every website, Vercel's servers see your IP address and browser type when your device downloads the app, and may keep this in logs for a limited time, for security and to keep the site running, under Vercel's privacy policy: https://vercel.com/legal/privacy-policy. We do not use these logs to find out who you are, and we do not combine them with anything else.
items: **Analytics are switched off.** We do not use Vercel Analytics, Google Analytics or any other tracker.
Fonts and pictures are part of the app, so your browser does not contact Google or other services.

The **Stats** page only shows counts of public GitHub issues (mistake reports). We read them from GitHub once a week when the site is built, so on that page your browser does not contact GitHub: it only downloads a small file from this site.

sections.title: How long we keep things
items: **On our side: nothing**, because we don't receive anything about you.
Reports on GitHub stay public until they are deleted. We delete any report that contains personal details as soon as we see it.

If we later add our own report form, we will update this page **before** it goes live. The plan is: no name or email fields, IP addresses used only for a moment to stop spam (never saved), server logs deleted within 14 days, and reports deleted within 90 days after they are handled.

sections.title: Children and India's data protection law
intro: LifePeek is made for school students. India's **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act)** protects personal data, with extra care for children. We follow it by not collecting personal data at all, so there is nothing to ask parents' consent for. If this ever changes, we will update this page first.

sections.title: Contact (grievances)

outro: Maintainer: {{name}} (GitHub: @Sarthaks-24). We aim to reply within 7 days.

Times and blood-sugar values are typical ranges and vary a lot between people. **It is not medical advice.** Do not use it to make health, diet or medical decisions. limits.glucoseTail: After big, fatty meals the model shows a small, slow tail; real bodies usually settle a little sooner.
limits.glucoseBand: The shaded band is a best guess of how much healthy people differ.
limits.energyInAtwater: Each gram of carbohydrate or protein counts as 4 kcal and each gram of fat as 9 kcal, so the total can be a little different from the food label. These standard numbers already allow for the bit of food the body cannot take in. The model also counts only what was taken in, so that bit is left out twice and energy coming in reads a few per cent low. The small amount of energy in fibre is not counted.
limits.energyUsedResting: This is a formula for a resting adult (the ICMR-NIN 2020 reference adult, 65 kg), not a measurement. It does not change with the meal.
limits.backToBase: "Back near the before-meal level" means within 5 mg/dL of it.
limits.glucoseSameHighest: More of the same food or drink does not raise the highest point here, only how long blood sugar stays up: the stomach lets food out at a steady rate (about 2 kcal a minute for a sugary drink), whatever the amount. The model leaves out anything else a bigger portion might do to the highest point in real people.
limits.steadyEmptying: The model lets food out of the stomach at a steady rate until it is empty. So after a big meal the food in the stomach falls in a straight line, and blood sugar and energy coming in stay level for hours, then fall within about an hour. Real stomachs usually slow down near the end, so the fall is gentler. After 6 hours the time axis is squeezed (the tinted part on the right), which makes the fall look steeper still.

adult-ref.desc: Based on the ICMR-NIN 2020 reference adult man (65 kg), at rest. Digestion times come from studies of adults.
